newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks fall for second day.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks fall for second day.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Thursday as the market extended into a second day its consolidation after Tuesday's record close.
At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 30.79 points at 6,989.34, having retreated from Tuesday's high of 7,067.46.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 13-9 on volume of 265 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said there were signs the dollar had topped out in the short-term, and this could end the stampede of foreign money into U.S. markets.
Cautious comments by Goldman Sachs strategist Abby Cohen gave investors a bit of additional incentive to take profits, but market watchers said this would have happened anyway.
The Nasdaq Composite Index was down 9.47 points at 1356.11 reflecting a mixed technology sector and a sell-off in the stock of Intel Corp.

"We are following up on the late weakness yesterday. The major indices are in the stratosphere, techs continue to trade in a volatile fashion, with market leadership stocks coming in for some profit-taking," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "Near-term, we're in for a little tough sledding."
The American Stock Exchange index was up 0.64 at 599.79.
Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. said there was evidence that the dollar had topped out in the near-term.
"If this proves to be true, you will see an end to the desperate stampede of foreign money into American financial instruments," he said.
In New York trading, the dollar fell to 122.75 Japanese yen from 124.43 yen late Wednesday, and to 1.6855 German marks from 1.6980 marks.
Metz said the bond market also appeared to have run out of steam, highlighting the overvaluation of the stock market.
"The earnings outlook is still good, but it is mixed in some sectors. Some high tech companies are saying that growth will be there this year, but that expectations are too optimistic," he said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was off 13/32, raising its yield to 6.61 percent from 6.58 percent Wednesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Analysts said investors might be using comments by Goldman Sachs' Cohen as a pretext for taking profits. Cohen adjusted her bullish view and said the stock market could be heading for a trading range.
The comments were made last Friday in a fax to clients but became the focus of interest again after the Wall Street Journal featured them Thursday.
"Her comments certainly aren't helping the market today," Metz said.
But Prime Charter's Bleier said that there was nothing new in what the Journal reported.
"This is not new news. This is only new for the newspapers, not for the market," he said.

Intel the most actively traded Nasdaq stock, fell 2-1/2 to 151-3/8 while its rival competitor Cyrix Corp. was up 4-3/8 at 29-7/8 on positive expectations for the company's new computer chip designed for use in lower-cost personal computers.
